lessons.briefing:
A 100 W solar panel costs KSh 7 000–10 000 in Nairobi (2025). Understanding what
that number actually buys — and what it does not — is the difference between a system
that runs a household for 15 years and one that fails in 18 months. This day decodes
the photovoltaic effect, reads a panel datasheet correctly, and calculates the right
tilt angle for any location in Kenya or East Africa.
lessons.briefingSw:
Paneli ya jua ya wati 100 inagharimu KSh 7,000–10,000 Nairobi (2025). Kuelewa
kinachonunuliwa kwa pesa hiyo — na kinachokosekana — ni tofauti kati ya mfumo
unaoendesha nyumba kwa miaka 15 na unaoshindwa ndani ya miezi 18.
lessons.contentMd:
## The Photovoltaic Effect

A silicon solar cell is a large semiconductor diode. It has two layers:
- **P-type** (positive): silicon doped with boron — has "holes" (electron absences)
- **N-type** (negative): silicon doped with phosphorus — has free electrons

At the junction between these layers, an electric field forms spontaneously.
When a photon with enough energy (≥ 1.12 eV for silicon) strikes the cell, it
knocks an electron free. The built-in electric field sweeps that electron toward
the N-side and the hole toward the P-side — creating a voltage (~0.5–0.6 V per cell)
and a current when an external circuit is connected.

**Key facts:**
- Each silicon cell produces ~0.5 V open-circuit; cells are wired in series to reach
  panel voltages (36 cells → ~18 V, which charges 12 V batteries)
- Current depends on cell area and irradiance (W/m²)
- A standard 100 W panel has 36 cells in series

## The I-V Curve

The I-V (Current–Voltage) curve describes every operating state a panel can be in:

| Point | Symbol | Meaning |
|-------|--------|---------|
| Short-circuit current | Isc | Max current when V = 0 (terminals shorted) |
| Open-circuit voltage | Voc | Max voltage when I = 0 (no load connected) |
| Max power current | Imp | Current at maximum power point |
| Max power voltage | Vmp | Voltage at maximum power point |
| Max power | Pmax = Vmp × Imp | Rated panel power |

**Typical 100 W panel datasheet values (STC):**
- Voc: 22.5 V | Vmp: 18.0 V | Isc: 5.98 A | Imp: 5.56 A | Pmax: 100 W

The **Fill Factor (FF)** measures how "square" the I-V curve is:
FF = (Vmp × Imp) / (Voc × Isc)

A good panel has FF > 0.70. Below 0.65 indicates cell degradation.

## STC vs NOCT — Why Your Panel Underperforms

All panel ratings are measured at **Standard Test Conditions (STC)**:
- Irradiance: 1 000 W/m²
- Cell temperature: 25 °C
- Air mass: AM1.5

Your roof in Nairobi at noon is NOT 25 °C. Cell temperature routinely reaches
45–65 °C. The **temperature coefficient of Pmax** for crystalline silicon is
approximately **−0.4 % per °C**.

At cell temperature 55 °C (30 °C above STC):
> Power loss = 30 × 0.4 % = **12 % power reduction**

A "100 W" panel delivers **~88 W** at typical Kenyan operating temperatures.

**NOCT (Nominal Operating Cell Temperature)**: the cell temperature at
800 W/m² irradiance, 20 °C ambient, 1 m/s wind. Typically 43–48 °C for
crystalline panels. Use NOCT conditions for real-world sizing.

## Panel Technologies

| Technology | Efficiency | Cost | Best use in Kenya |
|-----------|------------|------|-------------------|
| Monocrystalline (mono-Si) | 17–22 % | Higher | Best where space is limited; performs better in heat |
| Polycrystalline (poly-Si) | 15–18 % | Lower | Good value for large roofs |
| Thin-film (CdTe, CIGS) | 10–13 % | Variable | Better performance in diffuse/cloudy light — useful Coast and western Kenya |

**For most Kenyan households: monocrystalline** — better heat tolerance (lower
temperature coefficient: −0.35 %/°C vs −0.45 %/°C for poly) and more power
per square metre.

## Tilt Angle for Kenya

Optimal fixed tilt angle = local latitude (maximises annual energy yield).

| Location | Latitude | Recommended tilt |
|----------|----------|-----------------|
| Nairobi | 1.3° S | 5–10° (face north) |
| Mombasa | 4.0° S | 5–10° (face north) |
| Kisumu | 0.1° S | 5° (nearly flat) |
| Nakuru | 0.3° S | 5° |
| Eldoret | 0.5° N | 5° (face south) |

**Minimum tilt: 5°** even at the equator — to allow rainwater to wash dust off panels.
Dust reduces output by 5–25 % in dry season. A 5° tilt allows natural washing.

**Seasonal adjustment**: tilt toward the equator at latitude + 15° in the cooler
dry season (June–August in Kenya) captures more energy when the sun is lower.
This is optional for fixed residential systems.

## Shade Analysis

**One shaded cell can reduce the output of an entire series string by 30–75 %.**

Why: cells in series all carry the same current. A shaded cell produces less current;
the string current drops to match it. The shaded cell may also become reverse-biased
(a "hot spot") — generating heat, potentially cracking the cell or delaminating the module.

### Bypass Diodes
Modern panels have bypass diodes (typically 3 diodes per 72-cell panel, one per 24-cell
substring). When a substring is shaded, the bypass diode conducts — routing current
around the shaded cells at a cost of ~0.5 V drop instead of the full substring loss.

**Practical rule:** Avoid any shade on panels between 9 AM and 3 PM. Even a shadow
the size of a fist from a wire or tree branch costs significant energy over a day.

## Series vs Parallel Stringing

| Configuration | Voltage | Current | Use |
|--------------|---------|---------|-----|
| Series (+ to −) | Adds | Same | Increase system voltage (24 V, 48 V systems) |
| Parallel (+ to +, − to −) | Same | Adds | Increase current for 12 V systems |
| Series-parallel | Both increase | Both increase | Large arrays |

**For a 12 V system with 12 V nominal panels**: wire panels in parallel.
**For a 24 V system with 12 V nominal panels**: wire 2 panels in series.

Never mix panels of different wattage, Voc, or age in the same series string — the
weakest panel limits the entire string.

exercises.explanation:
Correct. (60 − 25) = 35 °C above STC. 35 × 0.38 % = 13.3 % loss. 200 × (1 − 0.133) = 173 W. At 165–175 W depending on exact conditions — this is the real-world operating range.

Why the other options are wrong: Panel ratings are at STC (25 °C cell temperature). Real-world cell temperatures in Kenya routinely reach 50–65 °C, causing significant derating. Higher temperature increases thermal noise in the semiconductor, reducing the built-in junction voltage. Output decreases with temperature for crystalline silicon. (Thin-film panels also derate, though slightly less.) There is no fixed 10 % rule. Loss is calculated from the actual temperature coefficient and the temperature difference from STC. Always use the datasheet coefficient.

options.text: 200 W — the rating is the rating regardless of temperature
Approximately 165 W — temperature derate of (60−25) × 0.38 % = 13.3 % applied
Approximately 220 W — hot panels produce more energy
About 180 W — there is a fixed 10 % loss for Kenyan conditions

exercises.prompt: A 200 W monocrystalline panel has a temperature coefficient of −0.38 %/°C. On a Mombasa rooftop the cell temperature reaches 60 °C. What is the expected output?

exercises.explanation: Vmp is typically 70–80 % of Voc. For a 12 V nominal panel: Voc ≈ 22 V, Vmp ≈ 18 V. A charge controller must track Vmp (MPPT) or be set below Voc (PWM) to extract useful power.
exercises.prompt: The maximum power point voltage (___) is always lower than the open-circuit voltage (Voc) on an I-V curve.

right.text: Maximum current at zero voltage (shorted terminals)
Maximum voltage at zero current (open terminals)
Rated power = Vmp × Imp at STC
Squareness of I-V curve = (Vmp × Imp) / (Voc × Isc)

exercises.prompt: Match each panel datasheet term to its correct definition.

lessons.outline:
1. The photovoltaic effect: how a silicon p-n junction converts photons to current
2. The I-V curve: Isc, Voc, Vmp, Imp, and maximum power point (MPP)
3. Reading a panel datasheet: STC vs NOCT conditions, temperature coefficients
4. Monocrystalline vs polycrystalline vs thin-film: which to choose in Kenya
5. Panel ratings in practice: 100 W STC does not mean 100 W on your roof
6. Tilt angle calculation for Kenya latitudes (equator to 4°S)
7. Shade analysis: the one-module-in-shade problem and bypass diodes
8. Series vs parallel stringing: when and why

lessons.briefing:
The battery bank is the most expensive, most failure-prone, and most misunderstood
component of any off-grid solar system. A 200 Ah lead-acid bank costs KSh 25 000–40 000
and should last 3–5 years with correct use — or 12 months with common mistakes. This day
covers chemistry, depth of discharge, C-rating, state of charge monitoring, and the
arithmetic of sizing a bank for a real Kenyan household.
lessons.briefingSw:
Benki ya betri ndicho kipande cha gharama zaidi, chenye kushindwa zaidi, na
kisichoelewa zaidi katika mfumo wowote wa jua nje ya gridi. Benki ya lead-acid
ya 200 Ah inagharimu KSh 25,000–40,000 na inapaswa kudumu miaka 3–5 kwa matumizi
sahihi — au miezi 12 na makosa ya kawaida.
lessons.contentMd:
## Battery Chemistry Comparison

| Chemistry | Types | Typical DoD | Cycle life | Cost (KSh/kWh) | Notes |
|-----------|-------|------------|------------|----------------|-------|
| Flooded Lead-Acid (FLA) | Wet/vented | 50 % | 300–500 @ 50 % DoD | 8 000–12 000 | Cheapest; requires topping up with distilled water; vents hydrogen |
| AGM (Absorbent Glass Mat) | Sealed | 50–60 % | 400–600 | 15 000–25 000 | Sealed; no maintenance; can mount at angle; more vibration-tolerant |
| Gel | Sealed | 50–80 % | 500–1 000 | 20 000–35 000 | Deep cycle; very heat-tolerant; charge slowly (10 % C rate max) |
| LiFePO4 (Lithium Iron Phosphate) | Sealed | 80–90 % | 2 000–5 000 | 35 000–60 000 | Expensive upfront; best lifetime cost; no memory effect; requires BMS |

**For most Kenyan off-grid systems today: AGM or FLA.**
LiFePO4 is becoming cost-competitive by 2025–2026 and is the long-term recommendation
where upfront capital is available.

## Key Parameters

### Capacity (Ampere-hours, Ah)
Capacity tells you how much charge a fully charged battery can deliver.
A 100 Ah battery can supply:
- 10 A for 10 hours, OR
- 5 A for 20 hours, OR
- 1 A for 100 hours

But this is only true at the rated discharge rate.

### Depth of Discharge (DoD)
DoD is how deeply you drain a battery before recharging. Lead-acid batteries are
damaged by repeated deep discharge:

| DoD | Lead-acid cycle life | LiFePO4 cycle life |
|-----|---------------------|-------------------|
| 30 % | 1 200 cycles | 5 000+ |
| 50 % | 500 cycles | 3 500 |
| 80 % | 200 cycles | 2 000 |
| 100 % | 50–100 cycles | 1 000 |

**Rule of thumb for lead-acid: never discharge below 50 % SoC (DoD = 50 %).**
Discharging to 80 % DoD regularly will destroy a lead-acid bank in under a year.

### The C-Rating
Batteries are rated at a specific discharge rate, expressed as a C-rating.

- **C20** (standard): full capacity over 20 hours → discharge current = Ah ÷ 20
- **C10**: discharge over 10 hours → higher current → *less* usable capacity
- **C100**: very slow discharge → slightly *more* usable capacity

A **100 Ah (C20) battery** at C10 rate (10 A discharge) typically delivers only
**85–90 Ah** — not 100 Ah. At C5 (20 A), it may deliver only **75 Ah**.

**Practical implication:** if you run a 300 W load (25 A from a 12 V bank) for
any significant time, size the bank assuming only 80 % of the rated Ah is available.

## State of Charge (SoC) Monitoring

### Open-Circuit Voltage (OCV) — most common method
Let the battery rest for **at least 2 hours** after charging or discharging, then measure voltage:

| SoC | 12 V FLA/AGM OCV | 12 V LiFePO4 OCV |
|-----|------------------|------------------|
| 100 % | 12.70–12.80 V | 13.4–13.6 V |
| 75 % | 12.40 V | 13.2 V |
| 50 % | 12.20 V | 13.1 V |
| 25 % | 12.00 V | 12.8 V |
| 0 % (empty) | 11.80 V | 12.0 V |

**Never use under-load voltage** to estimate SoC — it reads falsely low due to
internal resistance voltage drop.

### Hydrometer (FLA only)
Measures specific gravity (SG) of the electrolyte:
- Full charge: SG 1.265–1.280
- Half charge: SG 1.190–1.210
- Discharged: SG < 1.150 (sulfation risk — charge immediately)

Correct SG reading for temperature: +0.004 for every 10 °C above 25 °C.

## Sizing the Battery Bank

**Formula:**
> Battery bank (Ah) = (Daily load in Wh × Autonomy days) ÷ (System voltage × DoD × Battery efficiency)

**Variables:**
- **Daily load (Wh)**: sum of all load power × hours per day
- **Autonomy days**: how many cloudy/rainy days the system must sustain load without solar input
  (Kenya: 2–3 days for highlands; 1–2 days for coast/drylands)
- **System voltage**: 12 V or 24 V
- **DoD**: 0.50 for lead-acid; 0.80 for LiFePO4
- **Battery efficiency**: 0.85 (lead-acid round-trip); 0.95 (LiFePO4)

## Worked Example: Typical Kenyan Household

| Load | Power (W) | Hours/day | Daily energy (Wh) |
|------|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| 4 × LED lights (5 W each) | 20 | 6 | 120 |
| Phone charging × 3 | 15 | 2 | 30 |
| Radio | 5 | 8 | 40 |
| 32" LED TV | 40 | 4 | 160 |
| Phone charger standby | 3 | 16 | 48 |
| **Total** | | | **398 Wh/day** |

Sizing for **24 V system, AGM lead-acid, 2 days autonomy**:

> Bank (Ah) = (398 × 2) ÷ (24 × 0.50 × 0.85)
> = 796 ÷ 10.2
> = **78 Ah @ 24 V**

Nearest standard battery: **100 Ah @ 24 V** (two × 12 V 100 Ah batteries in series).

This leaves a 28 % safety margin — good practice as batteries age and lose capacity.

## Battery Wiring

### Series (to increase voltage)
Connect positive terminal of Battery 1 to negative terminal of Battery 2.
Bank voltage doubles; Ah stays the same.
→ 2 × 12 V 100 Ah in series = 24 V 100 Ah bank

### Parallel (to increase Ah)
Connect positive to positive, negative to negative.
Bank voltage stays; Ah doubles.
→ 2 × 12 V 100 Ah in parallel = 12 V 200 Ah bank

### Series-Parallel (both)
→ 4 × 12 V 100 Ah = 24 V 200 Ah bank
(First make two series pairs; then connect pairs in parallel.)

**Cable sizing to battery terminals:**
Use ≥ 35 mm² welding cable for battery interconnects if total current exceeds 50 A.
Undersized cables cause voltage drop, heat, and fire risk.

## Maintenance

### Flooded Lead-Acid Only — Monthly Checks
- Check electrolyte level: plates must be covered by ≥ 10 mm of electrolyte
- Top up with **distilled water only** (not tap water — dissolved minerals cause sulfation)
- Check SG with hydrometer; all cells should read within 0.030 of each other
- If one cell reads significantly lower: that cell may be failing — check for sulfation

### Equalisation Charge
Every 1–3 months, apply a controlled overcharge (≈ 15.5–16.0 V for a 12 V bank)
for 2–4 hours to equalise cell voltages and dissolve sulfation crystals.
Only for FLA batteries — never equalise AGM or Gel (will damage them).

### Temperature Compensation
Lead-acid capacity drops in cold weather and rises slightly in heat, but heat
accelerates degradation. Every 8.5 °C rise above 25 °C halves battery life.
In Nairobi highlands (cool nights): no concern.
In Mombasa/lowlands (hot): shade the battery bank; never enclose in a sealed box.

exercises.explanation:
500 W ÷ 12 V = 41.7 A. At C5 rate (~41 A for a 200 Ah bank), effective capacity drops to ~80% = 160 Ah. 50% DoD = 80 Ah. Time = 80 ÷ 41.7 ≈ 1.9–2.4 hours depending on actual derating.

Why the other options are wrong: This calculation ignores C-rate derating. At 41.7 A discharge from a 200 Ah bank (C4.8 rate), actual available capacity is only 75–80% of rated, not 100%. Ohm's law and power: P = V × I, so I = P ÷ V = 500 ÷ 12 = 41.7 A — not 500 A. The 500 W is the power, not the current. The C20 rate for a 200 Ah bank is 10 A (200 ÷ 20), not 20 A. At the actual discharge rate of 41.7 A (C4.8), the C20 capacity figure does not apply directly.

options.text: Current = 41.7 A; usable time = 4.8 hours (half of 200 Ah ÷ 41.7 A)
Current = 500 A; the battery would be damaged immediately
Current = 41.7 A; time = 10 hours because 200 Ah ÷ 20 A = 10 hours
Current = 41.7 A; usable time ≈ 2.4 hours (using 80% of rated Ah at this high discharge rate)

exercises.prompt: A household has a 200 Ah (C20) FLA battery bank at 12 V. The inverter is running a 500 W load. What is the discharge current and roughly how long before reaching 50% DoD?

exercises.explanation: From the OCV table: 12.00 V = 25% SoC, 12.20 V = 50% SoC. 12.05 V falls just above the 25% mark — battery is nearly empty and should be recharged immediately to prevent sulfation damage.
exercises.prompt: A technician measures 12.05 V on a 12 V FLA battery that has been resting for 3 hours. This indicates the battery is at approximately ___% state of charge.

right.text: Recommended maximum discharge — preserves 500 cycle life
Capacity when discharged fully over 20 hours
Critically discharged FLA cell — charge immediately
Controlled overcharge at 15.5 V to dissolve sulfation (FLA only)

exercises.prompt: Match each battery term to its correct definition or value.

lessons.outline:
1. Battery chemistry overview: lead-acid (FLA, AGM, Gel) vs lithium (LiFePO4)
2. Key parameters: capacity (Ah), voltage, depth of discharge (DoD), cycle life
3. The C-rating: why a 100 Ah battery is not always 100 Ah
4. State of Charge (SoC): voltage tables, hydrometer readings, coulomb counting
5. Sizing a battery bank: autonomy days, DoD, efficiency losses
6. Worked example: sizing for a typical Kenyan household (lights, phone, radio, TV)
7. Battery wiring: series, parallel, series-parallel; cable sizing to battery terminals
8. Maintenance: equalisation, watering, temperature compensation

lessons.briefing:
The charge controller is the brain of the solar system. It protects the battery from
overcharge and over-discharge, tracks the panel's maximum power point, and provides
load control outputs. Choosing the wrong controller — or sizing it incorrectly — wastes
10–30% of your available solar energy or destroys your battery bank. This day covers
PWM vs MPPT operation, controller rating arithmetic, and a complete system sizing
worksheet from load survey to component selection.
lessons.briefingSw:
Kidhibiti cha chaji ni ubongo wa mfumo wa jua. Inalinda betri dhidi ya kuchajwa
kupita kiasi na kutochajwa kupita kiasi, inafuatilia hatua ya nguvu ya juu ya paneli,
na kutoa matokeo ya udhibiti wa mzigo. Kuchagua kidhibiti kibaya — au kukipima vibaya —
inapoteza asilimia 10–30 ya nishati ya jua inayopatikana.
lessons.contentMd:
## PWM Controllers

A PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) controller works like a fast-switching switch between
the panel and the battery. When the battery is low, the switch is fully ON — the panel
connects directly to the battery. As the battery charges, the controller rapidly switches
ON and OFF (at 20 kHz or higher), reducing average current. When the battery is full,
the switch is OFF.

**Critical limitation:** The panel is effectively pulled down to the battery voltage.
A 12 V nominal panel (Vmp ≈ 18 V) is forced to operate at ~14.4 V (absorption charge
voltage). The panel operates well below its maximum power point.

**Efficiency:** PWM captures approximately 75–80 % of available panel energy.

**When to use PWM:**
- Small systems (≤ 200 W) where the cost saving is worthwhile
- Panel Vmp is close to battery voltage (12 V nominal panels on 12 V system)
- Budget-constrained installations

## MPPT Controllers

An MPPT controller uses DC-DC conversion circuitry to decouple the panel voltage from
the battery voltage. The controller actively sweeps the I-V curve and holds the panel
at its Vmp (maximum power point) regardless of battery voltage.

**How DC-DC conversion helps:**
If a 24 V panel (Vmp = 36 V, Imp = 5.56 A → 200 W) charges a 12 V battery:
- PWM forces panel to 14 V → power extracted ≈ 14 × 5.56 = **77 W** (60 % loss!)
- MPPT holds panel at 36 V, converts to 14 V: P_in = 200 W → I_out = 200 ÷ 14 ≈ **14.3 A at 14 V** (nearly 95 % efficient)

**Energy gain from MPPT vs PWM: 10–30 % more energy**, highest when:
- Battery is significantly lower voltage than panel Vmp
- Cold mornings (Voc rises in cold → MPPT captures the extra energy, PWM cannot)
- Higher voltage panels used (24 V, 36 V panels on 12 V battery)

**When to use MPPT:**
- Systems ≥ 200 W (efficiency gain pays for higher controller cost quickly)
- Mismatched panel voltage and battery voltage
- Cold climates or large seasonal temperature variation

## Controller Rating: Current Sizing

**PWM controller rating (A):**
> Rating ≥ Total panel Isc × 1.25

The 1.25 safety factor accounts for irradiance spikes above 1 000 W/m² (reflection
from clouds, snow, or bright surfaces can push irradiance to 1 200+ W/m²).

Example: 3 × 100 W panels, each Isc = 5.98 A, wired in parallel:
> Total Isc = 3 × 5.98 = 17.94 A × 1.25 = **22.4 A → use 30 A controller**

**MPPT controller rating (A output to battery):**
MPPT controllers are rated by their **output current** (to battery), not input current.
> Output current = (Total panel power × MPPT efficiency) ÷ Battery voltage
> = (300 W × 0.95) ÷ 12 V = **23.75 A → use 30 A MPPT**

**MPPT input voltage (Voc) rating:**
The controller's maximum input Voc must exceed the array open-circuit voltage, including
cold-temperature correction (Voc rises when cold):

> Cold Voc = Voc_STC × [1 + (Temp_coeff_V × (T_min − 25))]

For a Nairobi panel with Voc = 22.5 V and Temp_coeff = −0.30 %/°C at T_min = 10 °C:
> Cold Voc = 22.5 × [1 + (−0.003 × (10 − 25))] = 22.5 × 1.045 = **23.5 V**

Three such panels in series: 23.5 × 3 = **70.5 V → use a controller rated ≥ 75 V Voc**

## Load Survey: Auditing Household Loads

A load survey is the foundation of correct system sizing. Many installations fail
because loads are underestimated.

**Steps:**
1. List every electrical device in the household
2. Record rated power (from label or measured with clamp meter)
3. Estimate realistic daily hours of use (interview family members)
4. Add 10–15 % for cable losses, inverter losses, and forgotten loads

**Common underestimated loads in Kenya:**
- Mobile chargers: each phone draws 10–18 W for 1.5–2 hours per charge; most households
  charge 3–5 phones daily
- Security lights (if LED PIR): 8–12 W, may run 8–10 hours per night
- Hair clippers/dryers: 200–500 W — a single weekly use = 100–250 Wh/week ÷ 7 = 14–36 Wh/day
- Refrigerator: 60–150 W average but runs 8–12 hours/day cycling = 480–1 200 Wh/day
  (a fridge alone may require a complete system upgrade)

## Panel Array Sizing

**Formula:**
> Panels needed = Daily load (Wh) ÷ (Peak Sun Hours × Panel Wattage × Derating factor)

**Peak Sun Hours (PSH) for Kenya** (average annual; use lowest month for conservative design):

| Location | Annual avg PSH | Lowest month PSH |
|----------|----------------|-----------------|
| Nairobi | 5.5 | 4.5 (July) |
| Mombasa | 5.8 | 4.8 (May) |
| Kisumu | 5.2 | 4.0 (July) |
| Garissa | 6.5 | 5.5 |
| Eldoret | 5.3 | 4.2 (August) |

**Derating factors (multiply together):**
- Temperature derate: 0.87 (≈ 13 % loss at 55 °C cell temp, monocrystalline)
- Dust / soiling: 0.92 (8 % loss average; more in dry season)
- Cable losses: 0.97 (3 % if wired correctly)
- Combined derate: 0.87 × 0.92 × 0.97 = **0.78**

## Complete Worked Example: Rural Household System

**Load survey result:** 400 Wh/day (from Day 2 example)

**Battery bank (from Day 2):** 100 Ah @ 24 V AGM, 2 days autonomy

**Panel sizing (Nairobi, 24 V system, using lowest month PSH = 4.5 h):**
> Panels = 400 Wh ÷ (4.5 h × 100 W × 0.78) = 400 ÷ 351 = **1.14 panels**
> → Use **2 × 100 W panels** (114 % of minimum — good margin for cloudy days)

Total array: 200 W; Vmp = 36 V (two 18 V panels in series for 24 V system); Isc = 11.96 A

**Controller selection (MPPT for 200 W system):**
> Output current = (200 × 0.95) ÷ 24 = 7.9 A → use **10 A MPPT** (minimum)
> Input Voc (cold): 23.5 V × 2 panels in series = 47 V → controller Voc rating ≥ 50 V

**Recommended:** Renogy Rover 10 A MPPT (Voc input 50 V, widely available Kenya); cost KSh 4 000–6 000

## Wiring Order — Critical for Controller Safety

**Correct sequence when connecting:**
1. Connect battery to controller first (controller initialises, detects battery voltage)
2. Connect panels to controller second (controller now knows what voltage to regulate to)
3. Connect loads last

**Correct sequence when disconnecting:**
1. Disconnect loads
2. Disconnect panels
3. Disconnect battery

**Never connect panels to MPPT controller without battery connected** — the controller
has no voltage reference and may be damaged by the panel's open-circuit voltage.

**Never short-circuit the panel output** — solar panels are current sources; shorting
causes full Isc to flow, potentially burning cables or the controller input.

exercises.explanation:
Two 44 V panels in series = 88 V Voc (plus cold temperature correction ≈ 91 V). A 100 V Voc rated MPPT is correct. Output current: (400 W × 0.95) ÷ 24 V = 15.8 A → 20 A MPPT is the correct minimum rating.

Why the other options are wrong: Two 24 V panels in series gives an array Voc of 88 V. A 30 A PWM controller rated 12/24 V typically has a maximum input of 55 V — it would be instantly destroyed by 88 V. Also, PWM would force the 36 V Vmp panels to charge at 28 V, wasting 22 % of power. The output current calculation is correct (16.7 A) but a 10 A controller is undersized. Always select the next standard size above calculated minimum: 20 A. A 10 A controller would overheat and fail. Solar panels do not self-regulate. Without a charge controller, panels will overcharge the battery to Voc (88 V for this series string), destroying it within hours.

options.text: A 20 A MPPT controller with Voc input rating ≥ 100 V and output current ≥ 16 A
A 30 A PWM controller rated 12/24 V
A 10 A MPPT controller — two 200 W panels = 400 W which at 24 V is only 16.7 A
No controller needed — two panels in series automatically regulate voltage to 24 V

exercises.prompt: A customer has two 200 W, 24 V nominal panels (Vmp 36 V, Voc 44 V, Isc 5.8 A) wired in series connected to a 24 V AGM battery bank. Which controller is correct?

exercises.explanation: The battery must be connected first so the MPPT controller can detect the system voltage and initialise correctly. Connecting panels first to an MPPT without a battery can expose the controller to full Voc with no load — potentially damaging the input stage.
exercises.prompt: When installing a solar system, the correct first connection is: battery to controller. The second connection is: ___ to controller.

right.text: Hours per day of 1 000 W/m² equivalent irradiance at a location
Combined loss multiplier for temperature, dust, and cable losses (~0.78)

exercises.prompt: Match each system sizing parameter to its correct description or formula.

1. PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) controllers: operation, losses, when to use

lessons.briefing:
DC wiring is where most solar systems fail — not the panels, not the batteries, but
undersized cables, loose connections, and missing fuses. A DC arc at 48 V carries
far more energy than an AC arc at the same voltage; DC does not have a zero-crossing
to extinguish the arc. This day teaches the voltage-drop formula, cable sizing tables,
fuse selection, earthing, and the professional wiring standards that prevent fires and
system failures in Kenyan solar installations.
lessons.briefingSw:
Uwiring wa DC ndipo mifumo mingi ya jua inashindwa — si paneli, si betri, bali waya
ndogo, miunganisho huru, na fyuzi zilizokosekana. Arc ya DC kwa 48 V hubeba nishati
zaidi sana kuliko arc ya AC kwa voltage ile ile; DC haina sifuri ya kuvuka kuzima arc.
lessons.contentMd:
## DC vs AC Wiring — Why DC Is Harder

In AC systems, current reverses direction 50 times per second (50 Hz). An arc formed
by a loose connection or a fault is naturally extinguished every time the current
passes through zero (100 times per second). DC current does not reverse — an arc at
12 V, 24 V, or 48 V sustains itself indefinitely, burning through insulation and
igniting cable jackets.

**Implications for DC solar wiring:**
- Cable sizing must be more conservative (continuous current vs AC intermittent)
- Fuses must be DC-rated (AC fuses do NOT reliably interrupt DC arcs at rated current)
- Circuit breakers must be DC-rated and marked for the system voltage
- Connections must be mechanically secure and low-resistance — not just hand-tight

## Voltage Drop: The 3 % Rule

Voltage drop in DC cables causes power losses, false low-voltage shutdowns, and
controller errors. The standard for solar wiring:

**Maximum voltage drop:** 3 % for main system cables; 1 % for short runs.

At 12 V: 3 % = 0.36 V drop acceptable.
At 24 V: 3 % = 0.72 V drop acceptable.
At 48 V: 3 % = 1.44 V drop acceptable.

**Voltage drop formula:**

> ΔV = (2 × L × I × ρ) ÷ A

Where:
- ΔV = voltage drop (V)
- L = one-way cable length (m)
- I = current (A)
- ρ = resistivity of copper = 0.0175 Ω·mm²/m
- A = cable cross-sectional area (mm²)

**Rearranging to find required cable area:**

> A (mm²) = (2 × L × I × 0.0175) ÷ ΔV_max

### Example
Battery bank to inverter: 24 V system, 1 000 W inverter (max current = 1 000 ÷ 24 = 41.7 A),
cable run = 3 m (one-way), max ΔV = 0.72 V (3 % of 24 V):

> A = (2 × 3 × 41.7 × 0.0175) ÷ 0.72 = 4.375 ÷ 0.72 = **6.1 mm²**
> Use **10 mm² cable** (next standard size up; gives safety margin and lower operating temp)

## Cable Sizing Quick-Reference Table (12 V DC, 3 % drop, ≤ 5 m run)

| Current (A) | Min cable area | Typical use |
|-------------|---------------|-------------|
| 10 A | 2.5 mm² | LED lighting circuits, small loads |
| 20 A | 4.0 mm² | Charge controller to battery |
| 30 A | 6.0 mm² | Panel string to controller (MPPT) |
| 50 A | 10 mm² | Battery to inverter (≤ 500 W at 12 V) |
| 80 A | 16 mm² | Battery to inverter (≤ 800 W at 12 V) |
| 100 A+ | 25–35 mm² | Large inverter or battery interconnect |

**Temperature derate:** if cable runs through conduit, wall cavity, or bundles, derate
by 0.75× (select next larger cable size).

**Always use tinned copper cables** for battery connections — untinned copper oxidises
at the battery terminal, increasing resistance and causing heat buildup.

## Fuse Selection

Every positive conductor **leaving the battery** must be fused as close to the battery
as possible (within 150 mm / 6 inches ideally; maximum 300 mm / 12 inches).

**Why close to the battery?** The fuse protects the cable from the battery's fault
current capability (a large lead-acid bank can deliver 1 000+ A into a dead short).
Without a fuse, a shorted cable will glow red and ignite before the connection fails.

**Fuse rating rule:**
> Fuse rating = 125 % of maximum continuous current (next standard size up)

| Circuit | Max current | Fuse rating |
|---------|------------|-------------|
| Panel string (PWM, 12 V, 200 W) | 200 ÷ 12 = 16.7 A | 20 A |
| Battery to controller | Controller output rating | Match controller rating |
| Battery to inverter (300 W @ 12 V) | 25 A | 30 A |
| Battery to inverter (1 000 W @ 12 V) | 83 A | 100 A |
| Battery to inverter (1 000 W @ 24 V) | 41.7 A | 50 A |
| DC load circuit (LED lights) | 10 A | 15 A |

**Fuse types for DC solar systems:**
- **ATC/ATO blade fuses** (auto fuses): suitable for circuits ≤ 30 A; cheap; available everywhere
- **ANL/BF fuses**: for high-current battery connections (50–400 A); bolt-in; DC-rated
- **MIDI fuses**: 30–200 A; compact; widely used in solar installations
- **Circuit breakers (DC-rated)**: allow resetting without replacing; specify voltage rating
  (a 12 V DC breaker is different from a 240 V AC breaker of the same current rating)

**Never use AC-only fuses in DC circuits** — they may not interrupt DC arcs at rated
current and can fail to protect the circuit.

## MC4 Connectors and Ring Terminals

### MC4 Connectors (Multi-Contact 4 mm)
The standard weatherproof connector for solar panel cables.

- **Rated:** 30 A, 1 000 V DC
- **IP67** rated — submersible to 1 m; suitable for outdoor use
- Connectors from different brands are not always cross-compatible — use matched pairs
- **Crimping:** use a proper MC4 crimping tool; never solder MC4 pins (voids weatherproof rating, creates brittle joint)
- After crimping, pull-test each pin — should require > 50 N (5 kg) to withdraw

### Ring Terminals (Battery connections)
- Crimp, don't solder: soldered terminals can develop high resistance if flux is not
  fully removed; mechanically weaker
- Use the correct crimp tool die size for the terminal and cable combination
- Torque battery terminals to manufacturer spec — typically 8–12 N·m for M8 bolt terminals
- Apply petroleum jelly or terminal grease to prevent corrosion after tightening

## Earthing and Bonding

**Why earth a DC solar system?**
1. Limits voltage on exposed metal parts to safe levels in case of insulation fault
2. Allows fault current to flow through the earth path, blowing a fuse rather than
   through a person
3. Reduces radio frequency interference (RFI) in communications equipment

**What to earth:**
- All metal panel frames → earth wire → earth rod
- Charge controller case (if metal)
- Battery negative terminal (negative earthing — most common in 12/24 V systems)
- Inverter chassis

**Earth rod:** 1.2 m copper-clad steel rod driven into moist ground; tested with
earth resistance meter; target < 10 Ω (for lightning protection systems < 1 Ω)

**Negative earthing:** connect battery negative to earth rod via a dedicated green/yellow
earth conductor (≥ 6 mm² for systems up to 24 V, 100 A)

## DC Distribution Board Layout

For systems with multiple loads (lights, phone charger, TV, security light),
a DC distribution board prevents a jungle of wires from the controller.

**Components:**
- Positive bus bar: copper bar with multiple terminals; all positive leads connect here
- Negative bus bar: same, for negatives
- Individual fuses or MCBs (DC-rated) for each circuit — allows isolating one circuit
  without shutting down the whole system
- Main circuit breaker between battery and bus bar (allows shutting down entire system safely)

**Labelling:** every cable and circuit must be labelled — function (LIGHTS, TV, PHONE),
current rating, and fuse size. Use cable tie labels or heat-shrink markers.

## Common Wiring Faults (Pre-Energisation Checklist)

Before connecting the battery, verify:

| Check | Tool | Pass criterion |
|-------|------|----------------|
| No short circuit on DC bus | Multimeter (Ω mode) | > 1 MΩ between + and − |
| Correct polarity on all terminals | Multimeter (V mode) | Positive to positive, negative to negative |
| MC4 connectors locked and clicked | Physical check | Audible click; cannot pull apart by hand |
| All ring terminals tight | Torque check | No rotation under 5 kg·m hand torque |
| Fuses all rated correctly | Visual check | Fuse markings match design |
| Earth continuity | Multimeter (Ω mode) | < 1 Ω from panel frame to earth rod |
| No cable runs in tight bends < 5× cable diameter | Visual check | No kinks; no insulation damage |

exercises.explanation:
Correct. ΔV_max = 3% of 12 V = 0.36 V. A = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 0.36 = 7.0 ÷ 0.36 = 19.4 mm². Next standard cable size above 19.4 mm² is 25 mm², though 16 mm² is the minimum many installers use with derating safety margin at shorter runs. Strictly 25 mm² is safest.

Why the other options are wrong: 2.5 mm² at 50 A over 4 m gives ΔV = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 2.5 = 7.0 V — nearly 58% voltage drop. This would cause the inverter to shut down immediately on low-voltage protection. There is no universal standard cable size. Sizing depends on current and cable length. 6 mm² at 50 A over 4 m: ΔV = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 6 = 11.7% drop — far above the 3% limit. The voltage drop formula applies at all cable lengths. At 50 A and 10 mm²: ΔV = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 10 = 0.70 V = 5.8% — still above the 3% limit for a 12 V system.

options.text: 2.5 mm² — sufficient for 50 A in short runs
6 mm² — this is the standard cable for all solar installations
10 mm² — the voltage drop formula is unnecessary for runs under 5 m
16 mm² — calculated as A = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 0.36 = 19.4 mm², use next size up

exercises.prompt: A 12 V solar system has a 600 W inverter drawing 50 A maximum. The cable run from battery to inverter is 4 m one-way. Maximum allowed voltage drop is 3%. What minimum cable area should be used?

exercises.explanation: The 300 mm (12 inch) maximum rule ensures the unprotected cable section is too short to ignite before the fuse blows. Closer is always better — 150 mm is ideal. Fuses placed at the load end only protect the load, not the cable run from the battery.
exercises.prompt: Every fuse on a DC solar system must be placed within ___ mm of the positive battery terminal to protect the cable from the battery's full fault current.

right.text: IP67, 30 A / 1 000 V DC; weatherproof panel-to-cable connection
High-current bolt-in DC fuse for battery-to-inverter protection (50–400 A)
Low-cost automotive fuse for circuits up to 30 A
Resettable overcurrent protection; must specify DC voltage rating explicitly

exercises.prompt: Match each DC wiring component to its correct specification or use.

lessons.briefing:
A KSh 600 digital multimeter in the hands of someone who knows how to use it can
diagnose 90% of solar system faults in 20 minutes. A KSh 80 000 system left to a
guesser will fail and not be repaired. This final day of the solar unit teaches the
complete commissioning sequence for a new installation and a systematic fault-finding
methodology for diagnosing every common failure mode: no charge, low voltage, dead
loads, and battery that won't hold charge.
lessons.briefingSw:
Multimeter ya digital ya KSh 600 mikononi mwa mtu anayejua kuitumiaa inaweza
kutambua asilimia 90 ya hitilafu za mfumo wa jua katika dakika 20. Mfumo wa
KSh 80,000 ulioacha kwa mkisia utashindwa na hautarekebishwa.
lessons.contentMd:
## Multimeter Functions for Solar Technicians

A basic digital multimeter (DMM) measures:

| Function | Symbol | Solar use |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| DC Voltage | V⎓ or VDC | Battery voltage, panel Voc, controller output |
| AC Voltage | V~ or VAC | Inverter output verification |
| DC Current (clamp adapter) | A⎓ | Panel Isc, charge current, load current |
| Resistance | Ω | Cable continuity, fuse integrity |
| Continuity beep | ))) | Fast cable continuity check (beeps when resistance < ~30 Ω) |
| Diode test | ▷⎸ | Testing bypass diodes in panels |

**Clamp meter vs inline ammeter:**
- Clamp meters measure current without breaking the circuit — clamp around one conductor
- For DC clamp accuracy: zero the clamp away from any conductors first; only clamp around one conductor (not both)

## Safe Multimeter Practice

**Rules that prevent injury:**
1. **Always connect COM (black) lead first, disconnect last** — avoids accidental shorts
2. **Select the correct range or use AUTO range** before measuring — connecting a 200 V panel Voc to a 20 V DC range will damage or destroy the meter
3. **Never measure resistance or continuity on a live circuit** — put batteries, panels, and the controller on isolation first
4. **Use the correct input jack:** current is measured through the **A input** (with its own fuse), not the V/Ω input — measuring current through the V/Ω terminals causes a dead short
5. **Inspect leads before use** — cracked insulation on a multimeter lead is a shock and short-circuit risk; replace any damaged leads

## Commissioning Sequence: New Installation

Follow this exact sequence for every new installation. Deviating from the order risks
damaging controllers, batteries, or panels.

### Step 1 — Pre-connection checks (no battery, no panels connected)
- Inspect all cable terminations — tug-test every ring terminal and MC4 connector
- Measure resistance between positive and negative busbars: must be > 1 MΩ (no short)
- Verify fuse ratings match design
- Verify all cable labels match wiring diagram

### Step 2 — Connect battery to controller
- Connect battery negative to controller BAT− first
- Connect battery positive to controller BAT+ second
- Controller display should illuminate and show battery voltage
- Verify: multimeter DC voltage at controller BAT terminals = battery resting voltage ± 0.1 V

### Step 3 — Verify battery voltage
- Multimeter on controller display ≈ 12.5–13.0 V (charged AGM/FLA at rest)
- If voltage < 11.8 V: battery may be discharged or faulty — charge externally before proceeding

### Step 4 — Panel Voc test (before connecting to controller)
- Cover panels with an opaque cloth
- Connect multimeter DC voltage leads to panel output positive and negative
- Remove cloth: read Voc — should match datasheet Voc ± 5 %
- If reading is significantly lower than Voc: check for shade, damaged cell, or wiring error
- Cover panels again after test

### Step 5 — Connect panels to controller
- Panels still covered (covered = approximately 0 A output, safe to connect)
- Connect panel positive to controller PV+ first; panel negative to PV− second
- Remove covers
- Charge current should appear on controller display within 30 seconds of exposure to sunlight

### Step 6 — Verify charge current
- Clamp meter around positive cable from panel to controller
- Reading should match: (irradiance / 1 000) × panel Imp × number of panels × MPPT efficiency
- Example: noon (≈ 800 W/m²), 2 × 100 W panels, Imp = 5.56 A:
  Expected charge current = (800/1000) × 5.56 × 2 × 0.95 = **8.4 A**
- If reading is < 50 % of expected: shade, connection problem, or controller fault

### Step 7 — Connect loads and verify
- Turn on each load circuit individually
- Measure voltage at each load terminal — should be > 95 % of battery voltage
- Voltage significantly lower than battery voltage = undersized cable or loose connection

### Step 8 — Label, document, and hand over
- Photograph all connections, fuse board, and meter readings
- Record: battery voltage, charge current at noon, system configuration in a log book
- Explain to the client: what the controller display means, charge stages, and who to call

## Fault Tree 1: Battery Not Charging

```
Battery not charging?
│
├─ Is controller display ON?
│   NO → Check battery voltage at BAT terminals
│         < 10 V → battery dead or disconnected; check battery fuse
│         OK → controller may be faulty
│
├─ Controller ON, charge current = 0?
│   ├─ Cover panels → Voc test at PV input terminals
│   │   No voltage → check MC4 connectors, string fuse, panel cabling
│   │   Voltage OK → controller PV input may be faulty
│   └─ Voc OK but still 0 A → check for wiring reversal at PV terminals (reversed polarity
│       blows the PV input protection diode in most controllers)
│
└─ Charge current low (< 50 % of expected)?
    ├─ Check for shade or partial shade on any panel
    ├─ Clean panel surface (dust can cut output 15–25 %)
    ├─ Check panel string voltage at PV input = expected series Voc
    └─ Check ambient temperature — cold morning → Voc higher, MPPT catches it; normal
```

## Fault Tree 2: Load Circuit Not Working

```
Load not working?
│
├─ Measure voltage at load terminals (device unplugged)
│   0 V → circuit is open; go to next step
│   Full battery voltage → device is faulty; replace device
│
├─ Voltage 0 V — check fuse in circuit
│   Fuse blown → find and fix short circuit before replacing fuse
│   Fuse OK → check continuity from fuse to load terminal
│
├─ Continuity broken → open circuit in cable
│   Test each section: fuse holder → switch → junction → load terminal
│   Break found → repair or replace cable section
│
└─ All continuity OK, fuse OK, voltage 0 V at load?
    → Check controller LVD (Low Voltage Disconnect) — battery may be too low;
      controller has disconnected load output to protect battery
      Test: measure voltage between controller LOAD+ and LOAD−
      If 0 V from controller with battery connected: battery below LVD threshold
      Charge battery → loads should reconnect automatically
```

## Common Fault Causes in Kenyan Installations

| Symptom | Most common cause | Fix |
|---------|-----------------|-----|
| System worked for 6 months then stopped charging | Loose MC4 connector — vibration works connections free | Re-crimp or replace MC4 pair |
| Battery dies in < 12 months | Habitual deep discharge (DoD > 80 %) | Set controller LVD higher; educate client |
| Inverter shuts off under load | Undersized battery-to-inverter cable; voltage drop causes low-voltage cut-off | Upgrade cable; check connections |
| Controller shows error code | Overtemperature (controller in direct sun); short at PV input | Shade controller; check panel polarity |
| Low charge current in dry season | Dust accumulation on panels (can reduce output 20–25 %) | Clean panels with damp cloth; no detergent |
| FLA batteries consume water quickly | Overcharging — check controller charge voltage set point | Set absorption to 14.4 V, float to 13.6 V for 12 V FLA |

exercises.explanation:
Correct. Voltage is present at the panel but not at the controller PV terminals — the break is in the cable run between them. Inspect every MC4 connector for a full engagement click, check any string combiner fuse, and test continuity along the cable.

Why the other options are wrong: 43.2 V is 98% of the 44 V rated Voc — well within the ±5% acceptable tolerance. Panel Voc varies with temperature and manufacturing tolerance. The panel is fine. If the open circuit is between the panel and the controller, the controller PV input terminals will show 0 V regardless of the controller's health. Isolate the cable run first before concluding the controller is faulty. Panel Voc is an intrinsic property of the panel — it appears across the panel output terminals regardless of what is connected downstream, as long as the circuit is open. 0 V at the controller means the cable is broken or disconnected.

options.text: The panels are faulty — Voc should be exactly 44 V
There is an open circuit between the panel junction box and the controller PV input — check the MC4 connectors and any in-line fuse in that run
The controller is faulty — it should show panel voltage at its PV terminals
Normal — Voc only appears at the PV input when the controller is connected to the battery

exercises.prompt: During commissioning, you measure Voc at the panel output terminals (covered): 43.2 V (expected: 44 V). You then measure at the controller PV input terminals (same cable, covered): 0 V. What is the fault?

exercises.explanation: The V/Ω input has very high internal impedance (> 1 MΩ) — safe for voltage measurement. The A (ammeter) input has near-zero impedance to shunt maximum current through the measuring shunt resistor. Connecting the A terminals across a voltage source creates a near-short circuit, typically blowing the meter's internal fuse instantly.
exercises.prompt: When using a multimeter to measure DC current through an ammeter input, connecting the leads to the wrong terminals (V/Ω instead of A) causes a ___ which can blow the meter fuse or damage the circuit.
Commissioning practical: document multimeter measurements on your solar system.

rubric.criterion: Photo 1 — Battery resting voltage: multimeter in DC V mode, leads on battery terminals, reading clearly visible
Photo 2 — Panel Voc test: multimeter on panel output (or controller PV input), reading clearly visible
Photo 3 — Charge current: clamp meter around positive charge cable, reading visible (or screenshot of controller display showing charge amps)
All readings labelled with handwritten or typed labels in the photo or submitted notes
Readings are within expected ranges (battery 11.8–14.6 V; Voc within 5% of datasheet; charge current > 0 in daylight)

2. Safe multimeter practice: lead placement, range selection, avoiding common injuries
3. Commissioning sequence: the 8-step process for a new solar installation
4. Verifying panel output: Voc test, Isc test (with clamp meter)
